data.title: Johnson says 'we don't really need any investigation' on FAA ground stop
data.description:
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said there is no need for an investigation into the ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday, instead highlighting the need for “investment.”

“We don’t really need any investigation … we need further investment,” Johnson said during an interview with Fox News’s Saturday in America. “I mean, some of this equipment dates back to the eighties so it’s gotta be updated and that’s our responsibility. We’re gonna work to get it done.”

The FAA issued the nationwide ground stop around 4 p.m. EST on Friday. The rare protocol was in place for over four hours. The agency’s last widespread stoppage, which lasted approximately 90 minutes, was in January 2023.

The FAA lifted the stop at around 8:15 p.m., Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed during a White House press briefing Friday night.

Duffy attributed the incident to an overload of data on routers, with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin adding the “public was never in danger in this process.”

During the briefing, the officials called for a multi-billion-dollar investment into updating the U.S.’s “incredibly old” air traffic control systems.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Duffy said during the Friday night briefing. “Let’s not do a patchwork, a fix to a system that’s critical for every single family.”

“I want $50 billion,” he said.

Duffy in September asked Congress for $30 billion to fund new technology, control towers and airport improvements across the country.

In a press briefing Saturday morning, Duffy said a telecommunications line switch by a contractor may have started Friday’s FAA ground stoppage. He noted that an older copper wire was being replaced by a new fiber cable by contractor L3Harris.

More than 4,500 flights within, into or out of the U.S. were delayed as of Saturday afternoon with over 5,000 canceled, according to flight tracking website FlightAware. Total reported delays on Saturday crossed 15,000.

data.title: Fetterman: Naming Van Hollen majority leader 'would be troubling'
data.description:
Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) hinted that he could leave the Democratic Party if Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is elected as the Senate Majority Leader.

“Yeah, absolutely, it would be troubling if my caucus elects someone like Van Hollen that has really made his name being very anti … hostile to Israel,” Fetterman said when asked if there is a “red line” for him to walk away from the party, in a Fox News interview.

Fetterman’s remarks come after Van Hollen said Thursday that he would challenge Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for the role of the majority leader.

“In this election, Americans called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption,” Van Hollen wrote in a post on social platform X. “To deliver, we need new leadership. This isn’t about any one person – it’s about answering that call.”

Fetterman has previously warned that if the Democratic party becomes “the anti-Israel party,” he would leave.

In his recent Fox interview, Fetterman said, “If you are going to be angry or hostile towards any countries in the region, why not make that, you know, Iran, or Hezbollah or Hamas as well too?.”

Shortly after the midterm elections, where Democrats swept up the country in a “blue wave,” Schumer said that he expects to have the votes to be elected as the majority leader.

Several Democrats have said they would not back Schumer. This includes Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), as well as incoming senators Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.), Annie Andrews (D-S.C.), Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) and Troy Jackson (D-Maine).

The leadership bids come after the Democrats secured a sweeping victory in the midterm elections last week, taking control of both chambers of Congress. The party currently holds 55 Senate seats, after Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the state’s competitive Senate race.

The only state that has not called its Senate race is Alaska, where Democrat Mary Peltola is challenging Sen. Dan Sullivan (R).

data.title: Russia must be held accountable for its crimes
data.description:
Numerous reports allege that Russia is committing war crimes on a scale comparable to World War II. They reveal that the Russian army routinely tortures and kills Ukrainians taken prisoner and purposely targets civilian infrastructure, including apartment buildings, shopping malls, schools and utilities.

In the latest particularly disgusting display, Russian army units are reportedly hunting civilians with drones for sport. The Ukrainians refer to this as a “human safari.”

Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, international organizations, journalists, human rights groups and Ukrainian investigators have documented evidence of unlawful killings, torture, sexual violence, forced deportations, deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure and widespread violations of international humanitarian law. 

Holding Russian leaders accountable is important to provide justice to victims, establish a historical record and reinforce the principle that violations of the laws of war and humanitarian law should not go unpunished.  

Human Rights Watch reported in December 2025 that Russian authorities and military forces systematically tortured Ukrainian prisoners of war using physical and psychological abuse and holding detainees in inhumane conditions. The United Nations reported that evidence collected from hundreds of former prisoners indicated an extensive pattern of torture intended to break prisoners psychologically and physically. Such treatment violates Geneva Conventions protections for prisoners of war. 

International humanitarian law prohibits sexual violence against civilians and detainees. The U.N. Human Rights Office has reported over 1,000 cases of rape and sexual violence in areas occupied by Russian forces. Human Rights Watch has documented evidence of sexual violence in several territories occupied by Russian forces.

But the most egregious crime is what Russia is doing with Ukrainian children. The forced transfer and deportation of Ukraine’s children is a major area of international concern and a crime under several international conventions.

The Institute for the Study of War has documented extensive efforts to Russify Ukrainian children, which seem to be part of Putin’s effort to address Russia’s drastic population decline. Taking children from their homes and attempting to change their cultural identity or nationality during an armed conflict defies international laws designed to protect cultural heritage.

In March 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia’s commissioner for Children’s Rights, over alleged unlawful deportation and transfer of over 20,000 Ukrainian children to Russia. According to the court, there are reasonable grounds to believe the suspects bore criminal responsibility for these acts. 

In addition to Putin, the International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Russian Minister of Defense Sergei Shoigu and Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov, based on alleged responsibility for attacks against civilian infrastructure.

The scale of civilian suffering is ongoing and growing. According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, at least 2,514 civilians were killed and 12,142 injured during 2025, and civilian casualty rates have remained high throughout 2026. Since the beginning of the war, over 12,000 Ukrainian civilians have been verified as killed and about 25,000 injured.

Accountability for war crimes presents significant challenges. International courts must collect reliable evidence, establish individual responsibility and distinguish between intentional crimes and casualties resulting from lawful military operations. Nevertheless, investigations by the International Criminal Court, United Nations and independent human rights organizations have created substantial proof. 

Documented atrocities in Ukraine highlight the importance of international humanitarian law. War does not eliminate legal protections for civilians or prisoners, and military necessity does not excuse torture, intentional attacks on civilians, summary execution or unlawful deportation. 

Welcoming Russia back into the community of nations when this war ends should not be considered until the military and civilian leaders guilty of war crimes have been held to account. And inviting Russian officials to events held in the United States, and especially to the White House, is frankly disgraceful. 

John Fairlamb, Ph.D., is a retired Army colonel who served for 45 years as a commissioned officer and Department of the Army civilian in a variety of Joint Service positions formulating and implementing national security strategies and policies.

data.title: 5 things to know on the FAA groundings
data.description:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has air traffic control systems back online after a major telecommunications outage grounded all U.S. flights Friday evening.

The delay stranded passengers across the country and forced airlines to delay or cancel thousands of flights, a disruption that may take days to get back to normal. Those affected included everyday passengers, but also college football teams traveling to big matchups for Saturday.

Government officials have initially identified old equipment as the reason for the failure and have requested additional funding to modernize air traffic control systems.

Here are five things to know about the nationwide ground stop.

Millions of passengers face delays

Nearly 4,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. were delayed as of late Saturday morning, and more than 4,300 have been canceled, according to flight tracking website FlightAware.

Those delays and cancellations have only increased throughout the morning, and are concentrated at the busiest airports. Chicago’s O’Hare International Airport, Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport and New York’s John F. Kennedy (JFK) International Airport remain the three with the most disruptions.

Fifteen percent of all flights in Atlanta, the world’s busiest airport, have been canceled, with another nearly 20 percent delayed. Twenty percent of flights out of JFK have been canceled.

Airlines have begun accommodating passengers whose flights were disrupted. All four of the major airlines — Delta, United, Southwest and American — are waiving change fees for affected passengers, and Delta, United and Southwest are waiving fare differences to allow customers to change their flights at no additional cost.

Old communications systems seen as culprit

At a press conference Saturday, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that a wire switch may have caused the telecommunications outage.

Duffy said a contractor called L3Harris was replacing an old copper wire with a new fiber cable, and that the FAA was investigating to see if that was the cause.

“So what we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router?” Duffy said. “We haven’t determined what the fault was.”

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the agency has not identified any evidence of malice, such as a cyberattack.

“We see zero evidence of anything nefarious. It is an equipment issue,” Bedford told reporters. “When we have this root-cause analysis complete we will share it with you.”

College football teams race to make games

The travel disruptions hit right as college football teams were preparing to take off for anticipated Saturday matchups.

Games in the Big 12, Big Ten and Southeastern Conference were delayed Saturday, in some cases by several hours, due to the disruptions. The Ole Miss-Oklahoma game was moved to Sunday afternoon.

In the NFL, the league updated its officiating assignments to keep officials within driving distance of their homes amid the flight disruptions.

Trump officials plead for congressional dollars

At a joint press conference Friday night with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Duffy asked Congress to pass more than $50 billion in funding for modernizing air traffic control systems in the U.S.

“I want $50 billion,” Duffy told reporters. “Let’s finish this job: new hardware, new software, new telecommunication.”

Duffy has made a big push to modernize the FAA and air traffic control systems in his role as transportation secretary, pointing to decades-old systems that rely on old technology. Mullin echoed Duffy’s claims, calling for a “complete overhaul of the system.”

The transportation secretary shared his message to members of Congress.

“Give President Trump — give Duffy the money. Let them finish this job so we don’t have to do a press conference at 8:30 at night ever again,’” Duffy said.

Garcia, Jeffries signal oversight

As federal officials say they are investigating the cause of Friday’s incident, a key House Democrat is raising questions.

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the likely next chair of the House Oversight Committee, called the ground stop “quite disturbing” in an interview on MS NOW Friday.

“Whatever it is, I think deserves as much transparency as possible,” Garcia said.

The California Democrat has already pledged to investigate the president and his allies, which the White House vowed to aggressively respond to.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), the likely candidate for Speaker of the House, released a statement accusing the administration of “failed leadership.”

“American travelers deserve timely answers from the Trump Administration about how and why this happened and assurances that steps are being taken to ensure that our air travel system remains safe and functional,” Jeffries said.

data.title: Some Republicans say rising stars should sit out 2028 after midterm shellacking
data.description:
Republicans are actively talking about the wisdom of GOP candidates skipping the 2028 presidential race and focusing on 2032, arguing the political atmosphere in two years will be too poisonous for their brand. 

The discussions come in the context of sweeping losses for the GOP in last week’s midterms, which have a number of Republicans down in the dumps. 

There are also real worries over President Trump, whose popularity has hit new lows but whose policies and political discussions will loom over Congress and the White House for the next two years. 

That’s factoring into the decisions of some potential GOP presidential candidates. 

“How can a candidate run in 2028 when they have to criticize the policies of a sitting president with a large amount of sway with the Republican base?” said one GOP operative who is close to a lawmaker weighing a future presidential bid. “It’s a suicide mission.” 

“Unless there is a major shift in the direction of the country, where we end the war in Iran, reduce the cost of gas and groceries, and voters feel the White House is focused on their needs, I’m not sure any credible Republican candidate will run in 2028,” the operative said. “There is a strong feeling that the best chance a Republican has to win is in 2032 after these problems can be addressed and Trump is no longer a factor.” 

Vice President Vance, who is the front-runner for the GOP nomination, has also been weighing whether to launch a bid for 2028. But since the thumping Republicans received in the midterms, Vance’s allies have wondered quietly if 2028 is the right time for Vance, still just 42 years old, to run for the White House.  

“It may not be his time,” one former Trump aide said. “It’s going to be a tough time for any Republican to run for president in 2028 based on what happened last week.” 

CNN reported Friday that Vance has given serious consideration to not running for president in 2028. While the outlet said the vice president has “yet to make up his mind,” those in his orbit said he’s been mulling the future of MAGA while also thinking about his family and his four young children. Vance wants to be a central part of the rebuilding effort for Republicans but also is unsure “whether he should be the one to lead it,” the report said. 

Veteran GOP strategist Susan Del Percio said the uncertainty surrounding Vance’s political future and the reluctance of other Republicans to enter the race underscore the predicament facing the party. 

“Trump will be the downfall of any 2028 nominee because they have to be 100 percent MAGA, and pass the MAGA loyalty test and no one can do that because you don’t know what the president will be for or against at any given moment,” Del Percio said. “We talk about how Trump’s numbers can’t get any worse. But they can. This is only the beginning.” 

Trump has not endorsed Vance or any would-be candidate in the contest and allies say they don’t expect him to do so anytime soon.

Del Percio said that gives Vance an “out” not to run for president, if he chooses.

“The best scenario for JD Vance is to say he’s not running because he does not have the president’s endorsement,” she said. “If that’s the case, it allows him to bow out gracefully.”

On the other hand, Del Percio added, he could also use it as a way of securing the president’s endorsement and getting it early.

“It’s a way of softly forcing the president’s hand,” she continued. “If he does want to run, he has to get his endorsement and he needs to start running soon. He can’t leave room for speculation.”

It is, of course, early days after the GOP’s midterm disaster, and the political winds could change. After the 2024 elections, it was Democrats who were in the dumps, while Republicans imagined running Washington for some time.

Other Republican strategists involved in discussions about the upcoming election said the concerns about 2028 are real and that candidates are second-guessing the race. But they also said the GOP is hardly prepared to concede the next presidential election. Republicans will pour resources into the fight and mount aggressive campaigns, particularly in congressional races.

They’ll also be hoping that Democrats trip over themselves as they take command of the House and Senate. The GOP is hoping, and many Republicans say they are expecting, the Democrats in power to overreach, and potentially tarnish their own brand.

Yet at the same time, the presidential contest presents a different calculation. While Democrats are roaring to congressional power, the White House remains with Trump, leaving him with tremendous authority to run the country. That gives Democrats someone to run against for the next two years, too.

The mood right now in many GOP circles is dour on the 2028 cycle after the surprise wipeout in Texas, and Senate defeats in states such as Mississippi and South Carolina.

“Everybody is still in the fog of defeat but no one is confident that 2028 is going to be appreciably better,” said one national Republican consultant who worked on midterm races. “We’re gonna play, we’re gonna spend a ton of money, and we’re going to do better than we did because it was so bad this time. 

“But as far as flipping these institutions and winning the White House, no one thinks that’s in the cards for 2028,” the consultant said. 

One former Trump campaign aide disagreed with that assessment, saying that Republicans have time to figure it out in the coming months. 

“I know RNC members are specifically looking at how to rebound and win in 2028, which is why Jon Gruters is getting so much pushback in his effort to try to run for chair again and will likely lose,” the former aide said, referring to the chair of the Republican National Committee. “Giving up on 2028 when the Democratic Congress hasn’t even been sworn in strikes me as not only premature, but has to come from the same loser consultants who spent hundreds of millions of dollars to have the worst election in 50 years.”

Republicans acknowledge being worn down after the disastrous cycle.

There’s “massive donor fatigue” from the midterms, the GOP consultant said. Republicans also say they are also bracing for two more years of the Trump presidency, and some fear an administration that now includes Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff could harm the GOP brand.

“Donald Trump is not going to reinvent himself,” said one former Trump aide. “Does anyone think he’s going to change course? Does anyone think he’s going to be more conciliatory? He is doubling down with Stephen Miller.

“The general consensus is that we’re f‑‑‑ed until Donald Trump leaves office,” the former Trump aide said. 

As far as 2028 goes, the former aide said, “someone gets to be the sacrificial lamb, that’s how a lot of people are looking at it. Some candidates will do it to develop a national donor network, get their name out there and come back with a much better set of cards in 2032. 

“The only shot we have right now is if Democrats do a bunch of cooky s‑‑‑ and nominate a super progressive,” the former Trump aide said. “That’s the dream scenario for 2028.”

data.title: Stop the political warfare against Elon Musk — our very survival may depend on him
data.description:
I get that many on the left are angry with Elon Musk. But as with the thousands of people who either celebrated or rationalized the assassination of Charlie Kirk last year — including people within the U.S. government and military — I cannot help but think that many of those who harbor an unhinged hatred for the visionary entrepreneur are literally hopeful for his demise as well.

According to an NPR-PBS News-Marist poll released in October 2025, 30 percent now believe we “may have to resort to violence to get the country back on track … up 11 points since April 2024.” When did killing a fellow human being simply because of differing political views become so acceptable to so many? Most especially if there is a chance that one of those lives threatened could save humanity, should the worst happen to our planet? 

As someone who has long had one foot in the political world and the other in the space world, I am exceedingly happy that the contentious midterm election is now behind us, for a host of reasons. One reason is that despite the growing threats to investigate or even imprison Musk may free him up to devote much more of his brain power on how best to establish a large and permanent human presence in space.

The fact of the matter is that our species, at the direction of imperfect “leaders” living in bubbles of entitlement far from the working class of the world, has demonstrated an eagerness to wipe out wide swaths of humanity throughout history. The horrific war continuing to take place between Russia and Ukraine is just the latest example — a war that is littered with trip wires that could trigger a world-wide nuclear war. 

If that’s not terrifying enough, we also have, as the world witnessed during the COVID pandemic, the very real possibility of an evil laboratory virus killing us all, or the rise of a new robotic overlord?

With humanity at such a growing risk of extinction, don’t we want to hedge our bets and get some percentage of the human species permanently off the surface of Earth? Once upon a time, before the “Age of Trump” and hate before reason, Musk was really, really good at thinking of ways to get humankind permanently off the planet. For the sake of us all, we need to put hate aside and allow him to be that person again. 

Like him or not, agree with him or not, Elon Musk does have a once-in-a-century mind. The kind of mind that when it is freed from poisonous partisan nonsense, has the exceptionally unique ability to focus on ways to propel a large cross-section of humanity into the cosmos.

To that critical quest, more than years ago, Musk gave a keynote speech at the 67th International Astronautical Congress, where he spoke of his dream to colonize Mars in an effort to protect humankind from “certain doom.” 

He stressed: “Long term, it’s essential for preserving the light of consciousness. Eventually something will happen to Earth, hopefully not soon, either natural or man-made that would cause the end of civilization. The probable lifespan of civilization is much greater if we’re a multi-planet species.” 

Musk is correct. We all must recognize that, and allow him the time and peace of mind to figure out a way to place our species among the stars, before war, a virus, an asteroid or other cataclysmic event ends all life on Earth.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

data.title: New York sued over 'warning label' law for social media applications
data.description:
An internet trade group, representing 30 members including Google, YouTube, Facebook and Instagram, has sued the state of New York challenging its law that requires social media platforms ​to provide state-approved warning labels ‌for users.

NetChoice’s complaint said the state law violates the free-speech protections or First Amendment rights, Reuters reported.

The law, that was signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul (D-N.Y.) last year, requires social media platforms to warn about potential harm to younger users, the report said. It is scheduled to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

“Unlike a static warning on ​a product label, these warnings repeatedly interrupt users and ​block access ⁠to protected speech,” NetChoice noted.

Earlier this month, similar lawsuits were filed by Meta, TikTok and Google against California which argued that the state’s bipartisan “Digital Age Assurance Act,” violated both the First Amendment and the federal Communications Decency Act.

The Communications Decency Act protects online platforms from being sued over third party content. California’s Digital Age Assurance Act was also set to go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

The California law would ban social media platforms from providing “an addictive feed” to users under the age of 16. It would also require social media companies to “implement reasonable measures” to prevent minors from accessing such features.

The legal battles over children’s safety and social media have been brewing in recent months.

Last month, West Virginia sued TikTok and its parent company, ByteDance, alleging that the social media company violated state consumer protection laws by using addictive features to encourage excessive screen time among children.

The state also accused the platform of overstating the effectiveness of its parental controls while failing to address gaps that could allow predators to contact children.

In August, California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey faced Meta in a high-profile trial, as part of a coalition of 29 states suing the company for allegedly designing features to keep minors hooked on social media and deceiving parents about the safety of the platforms. Later that month, a $17 billion settlement was reached in the case.

Separately, Meta would have to pay Texas more than $1 billion over similar allegations, bringing the tech giant’s total payment sum to just more than $18 billion.

data.title: Pennsylvania, Wisconsin report additional deaths linked to measles
data.description:
The U.S. reached 10 measles deaths this year after additional deaths reported in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, a concerning sign as the previously eradicated disease makes a resurgence worldwide and in the U.S.

Measles cases have already reached more than 5,400 this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) dashboard — more than double the nearly 2,300 reported through the entirety of 2025.

Ninety-six percent of cases in 2026 are in unvaccinated individuals, compared to 93 percent last year.

Pennsylvania’s department of health confirmed that the newly added measles death, which brings the total to 7 deaths in the commonwealth, was in an unvaccinated person. Wisconsin said that a child had died but did not specify other details.

The Keystone State, with more than 1,500 cases, accounts for more than 1 in 4 cases reported in the entire country, according to the state’s dashboard.

Despite previously being eradicated in the U.S., measles has made a resurgence as vaccination rates have declined.

Pennsylvania issued a warning to doctors last month that the commonwealth had identified a case of congenital measles — measles transmitted from a mother to her newborn — for the first time in decades.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) were locked in a bitter dispute earlier this year after Shapiro said Kennedy, a longtime vaccine skeptic, was “spreading misinformation.” Kennedy said there was no evidence of that.

President Trump signed an executive order earlier this year recommending splitting the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three separate shots, claiming without evidence that it is “quite lethal.”

The CDC sent a “disease detective” to Pennsylvania in October to assist the state in responding to the outbreak.

data.title: A different kind of ticket-splitting
data.description:
Going into Election Day, we heard a lot about potential ticket splitting in Texas. Maybe Republican Gov. Greg Abbott would win reelection while voters rejected Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Senate race.

That didn’t happen. Both men lost.

But a different kind of ticket splitting may have emerged elsewhere, and it’s worth paying attention to.

Democrats had a wildly good night on Tuesday. Republicans got obliterated. But further down the ballot, voters in some states that flipped to blue approved ballot questions that don’t exactly line up with the Democratic Party platform.

In Washington state, where Republicans haven’t won a governor’s race since 1980, nearly 57 percent of voters supported an initiative to keep males out of girls’ K-12 sports.

In Colorado, voters favored two measures: one requiring sex-based eligibility for school and college athletics and another prohibiting certain gender-related surgeries for minors.

Arizona voters supported restrictions involving school sports, bathrooms, and locker rooms.

In North Carolina, voters approved measures limiting taxation authority and expanding voter ID requirements. Florida voters approved a property tax reduction, while voters in Nevada and Ohio backed voter ID requirements.

We usually think of ticket splitting as voting for a Democrat in one race and a Republican in another. But what about voting for all Democrats while supporting ballot questions that reflect a position more commonly associated with Republicans?

We don’t know how many individual voters did exactly that, but the results suggest something that tends to get lost in all the red-versus-blue election coverage.

Someone can be furious about gas prices, fed up with corruption, frustrated with the direction of the country, or simply repelled by the candidates and still want policies they believe are fair and sensible when it comes to children and schools.

And voting against a Republican doesn’t mean rejecting every position associated with conservatives, any more than voting for a Democrat means embracing every position associated with progressives.

And then there’s the quality of the candidates themselves. Some were deeply flawed, some ran lousy (and lazy!) campaigns, and some seemed to think dissatisfaction with the other party was a substitute for giving voters an actual reason to support them.

That’s what makes the ballot questions so interesting. In some places, voters were rejecting the candidates but supporting their policy positions. 

Ballot questions offer something candidate races rarely do: the chance to weigh in on an issue without having to accept everything else that comes with a politician. A vote for governor or senator is a package deal. You’re choosing someone based on a whole collection of issues, priorities, promises, and personal qualities. You might agree with a candidate on five things and still decide the sixth is a dealbreaker. A ballot question strips all of that baggage. It asks voters to make a decision about one policy, without requiring them to sign on to everything else associated with a candidate they can’t stomach.

These ballot question fights are not over. In Washington state and Colorado, opponents are already discussing legal challenges to the measures that voters supported. What happens when the people elected to govern a state disagree with the voters on a specific issue?

And similar ballot questions could be coming to a state near you. A group of citizens recently dropped off signatures in hopes of setting up a women’s sports referendum in Maine, a state where we just saw a six-term Republican incumbent lose her Senate seat.

The blue wave turned out to be a tsunami and that makes these ballot question results even more interesting. If we really want to understand the electorate in these midterms, we need to pay attention to both.

Winning an election and winning an argument are definitely not the same thing.

Erika Sanzi is the senior director of communications for Defending Education.

data.title: Musk: 'Critical deals will be lost' at Nvidia without Huang
data.description:
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on Saturday that Nvidia will lose “critical deals” after CEO Jensen Huang’s exit from the company following reports of his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

“Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” Musk wrote in a post on social platform X. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”

Huang’s resignation was announced Thursday following scrutiny over accusations stemming from a New York Times report in October that claimed American authorities discovered Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang illegally smuggled AI chips into China while developing a “close relationship” with the now-former Nvidia chief.

The resignation came a day after the Times reported Wednesday that Huang had a separate affair with a Nvidia executive who reported to him, citing five people who worked at the company.

Musk has previously hinted his support for the former Nvidia CEO, saying it “would be an honor” to hire him, prior to his resignation, in response to a post on X.

President Trump, in a Truth Social post, suggested that former Apple CEO Tim Cook should be the one to take Jensen Huang’s place, saying, “there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple.”

“A Legend replaces a Legend!” the president wrote in his post.

Following the initial Times report, Nvidia’s board had announced Sunday that it would initiate an independent investigation into the matter. On Tuesday, the company said it hired former acting U.S. Attorney Joon H. Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to conduct the investigation.

Huang admitted in a statement that he has been unfaithful to his wife, adding, “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” according to a report from Bloomberg. 

He was called by GOP lawmakers to appear in a joint, closed-door briefing on Nov. 18 to address concerns regarding Nvidia’s security protocols and his interactions with the alleged spy.
